title: Reducing self-supervised learning complexity improves weakly-supervised classification performance in computational pathology
authors: Tim Lenz, Omar S. M. El Nahhas, Marta Ligero, Jakob Nikolas Kather
text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools can assist pathologists in various tasks like tumor detection [1], disease classification [2] or prognosis [3] and has even enabled the extraction of clinically actionable insights from routinely available data [4]. Traditionally, the development of AI models for medical applications has relied heavily on manually annotated data [5]. Foundation models for computational pathology have proven to alleviate the need for annotated data as they are pre-trained on diverse datasets in order to be applied on various different use cases that are relevant for current research [6]. In order to obtain adequate foundation models, massive amounts of data and compute are utilized [7,8,9,10] to train large scale models like Vision Transformers [11]. The amount of training data can be substantially increased if the necessity of annotations is avoided. This led to the establishment of self-supervised learning methods [10]. Instead of focusing on few targets during training, self-supervised learning methods learn from inherent patterns and relationships in unlabeled data. Thereby, the capacity for generalization and adaptation to diverse tasks is amplified, while also surpassing the performance of models trained in a supervised manner [12,13,14,15]. Foundation models trained with self-supervised learning methods are often applied as encoders to compress the high-dimensional input data to its most important information content in the form of feature vectors. Those feature vectors are then applied on downstream classification tasks in a weakly supervised manner [4]. The rise of self-supervised learning methods alongside exponential hardware improvements enabled the training of increasingly capable foundation models. Nevertheless, current strategies are too resource-intensive as the data volumes, hardware requirements and overall costs are increasing rapidly to a point where only few institutions can contribute to methodological improvements in this field of research. This point is exemplified in recent studies, which required thousands of GPU hours to train their foundation models in computational pathology [8,1,9,10,7]. This resource intensive entry-barrier limits open-source advancements in non-resource abundant environments. Thus, we explore feasible solutions to train foundation models at scale on consumer-grade hardware. Our main contributions are as follows:

- \bullet To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first comprehensive ablation study that analyzes self-supervised learning complexity reductions in relation to weakly supervised classification performance on breast cancer related histopathology tasks.

- \bullet We improve over existing semantically relevant contrastive learning methods in computational pathology.

- \bullet We show that modifications in data volume, the self-supervised learning model architecure and the contrastive learning loss function improve the efficiency of self-supervised learning in computational pathology while surpassing state-of-the-art results. The findings of these adaptations enable the utilization of self-supervised learning in computational pathology in non-resource abundant environments.
